title: Justice Department Moves to Drop Lawsuit Over Alaska Senate Race, NBC News Reports
body:
The Justice Department on Thursday asked a federal appeals court to dismiss a lawsuit it filed in Alaska last month that sought to prevent the state from certifying the results of its 2022 Senate race. The petition, submitted by the Department’s civil division, argues that the case is “premature” and “lacks standing,” effectively withdrawing the administration’s attempt to intervene in an election that saw Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. The move comes after the Trump‑appointed officials who originally championed the suit faced mounting criticism and a rapidly shifting political landscape.

The original complaint, lodged in August, was an unprecedented effort by the federal government to block a state’s certification of a congressional election. It alleged that the Alaska Division of Elections had failed to follow “proper procedures” in handling absentee ballots and that the outcome could be challenged under the Constitution’s Elections Clause. The filing was widely viewed as an extension of the post‑2020 election litigation strategy that the Trump administration pursued in several swing states, aiming to overturn results that did not favor Republican candidates. In Alaska, the stakes were high: a loss for Sen. Dan Sullivan would have narrowed the GOP’s majority in the Senate, a scenario the administration was keen to avoid.

Legal experts say the Department’s sudden reversal underscores the fragility of the case. “The government’s standing to sue over a state’s certification process is tenuous at best,” noted constitutional law professor Elena Martinez of Georgetown University. “Even if the Department could argue a procedural defect, the courts have consistently ruled that election certification is a political question reserved for the states.” The Department’s appeal to the Ninth Circuit, which oversees Alaska, highlighted procedural deficiencies in the original filing, but it also signaled an acknowledgment that the lawsuit was unlikely to succeed on its merits.

Political analysts also see the withdrawal as a pragmatic concession. The Trump‑aligned faction within the Department, led by former Attorney General William Barr’s appointees, had been under pressure from both Republican lawmakers and the broader public to cease what many described as “politically motivated” litigation. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D‑NY) called the original suit “an abuse of power,” while some GOP senators expressed concern that the administration’s actions could erode confidence in the electoral system. With Peltola’s victory already certified by Alaska’s officials, the Department’s request to dismiss the case appears to be an effort to limit further damage to the administration’s credibility.

The broader implications of the episode extend beyond Alaska. The Justice Department’s brief foray into election oversight raised questions about the limits of federal authority in state-run elections. While the Constitution grants Congress the power to regulate federal elections, the day‑to‑day administration of ballots, counting, and certification remains largely in the hands of state officials. The Alaska lawsuit, therefore, tested the boundaries of that division of power and highlighted the potential for federal overreach in a highly polarized political environment.

Looking ahead, the case is expected to be resolved quickly, with the Ninth Circuit likely to grant the dismissal. The decision will close one of the last legal chapters of the post‑2020 election saga, but it will also leave lingering concerns about how future administrations might use the Department of Justice to influence electoral outcomes. As Congress and the courts continue to grapple with the balance between state autonomy and federal oversight, the Alaska episode serves as a cautionary tale about the perils of politicizing the nation’s most fundamental democratic process.
